source_text: Detestandi autem etiam illi sunt, qui dominum nostrum Iesum Christum matrem Mariam in terris negant habuisse, cum illa dispensatio utrumque sexum, et masculinum et femininum, honorauerit et ad curam dei pertinere monstrauerit non solum quem suscepit, sed illum etiam, per quem suscepit, uirum gerendo, nascendo de femina. nec nos ad negandam Christi matrem cogit, quod ab eo dictum est: quid mihi et tibi est, mulier? nondum uenit hora mea, sed admonet potius, ut intellegamus secundum deum non eum habuisse matrem, cuius maiestatis personam parabat ostendere aquam in uinum uertendo. quod autem crucifixus est, secundum hominem crucifixus est; et illa erat hora, quae nondum uenerat, quando dictum est: mihi et tibi quid est? nondum uenit hora mea, id est, qua te cognoscam. tunc enim ut homo crucifixus cognouit hominem matrem et dilectissimo discipulo humanissime commendauit. nec illud nos moueat, quod, cum ei nuntiaretur mater eius et fratres, respondit: quae mihi mater aut qui fratres et cetera? sed potius doceat ministerium nostrum, quo uerbum dei fratribus ministramus, parentes cum inpediunt, non eos debere cognosci. nam si propterea quisque putauerit non eum habuisse matrem in terris, quia dixit: quae mihi mater? cogatur necesse est et apostolus negare habuisse patres in terris, quoniam praecepit eis dicens: nolite nobis patrem dicere in terris; unus est enim pater uester, qui in caelis est.
thought_title: Christ's earthly mother and the hour of the cross
orientation: Augustine is still defending the full humanity of Christ, now against those who deny that the Lord Jesus Christ had Mary as his mother on earth.
pass_a_gloss: But those also are to be detested who deny that our Lord Jesus Christ had Mary as his mother on earth, since that earthly mission honored each sex, both male and female, and showed that not only the one whom he took up but also the one through whom he took up belonged to God's care, by acting as a man, by being born from a woman. Nor does what was said by him compel us to deny the mother of Christ: 'What is there to me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come,' but rather it warns us to understand that according to God he did not have a mother, the person of whose majesty he was preparing to show by turning water into wine. But that he was crucified, he was crucified according to man; and that was the hour which had not yet come when it was said: 'What is there to me and to you? My hour has not yet come,' that is, the hour in which I will know you. For then, crucified as man, he knew his human mother and most humanely entrusted her to the most beloved disciple. Nor should that move us, that when his mother and brothers were announced to him, he answered: 'Who is my mother or who are my brothers' and the rest? But rather let it teach that our ministry, by which we minister the word of God to brothers, when parents hinder it, they ought not to be acknowledged. For if anyone thinks for this reason that he did not have a mother on earth, because he said: 'Who is my mother?', he is forced by necessity also to deny that the apostle had fathers on earth, since he commanded them saying: 'Do not call anyone father to yourselves on earth; for one is your father, who is in heaven.'

choices.why: gerendo here means carrying out or performing the role of a man, not pregnancy; the phrase contrasts with 'nascendo de femina' and describes Christ's male role in the earthly mission
personam is the direct object of ostendere, and cuius maiestatis modifies it; Christ was preparing to show the person whose majesty he possessed

choices.english: Do not call anyone father to yourselves on earth
choices.why: nobis is dative of advantage, not the object of 'call'; the command forbids calling anyone on earth father for oneself, not calling the apostles father

choices.why: qua is ablative feminine agreeing with hora, and cognoscam is future; the hour of the cross is when Christ as man will know his mother in the full sense

choices.why: superlative adverb emphasizing the tender human care Christ showed at the cross, fitting Augustine's point about his true humanity

pass_b_english: We must also detest those who deny that our Lord Jesus Christ had a mother on earth, Mary. His earthly mission honored both sexes, male and female, and showed that God's care extends not only to the one he took up but also to the one through whom he took him up—by being a man, and by being born of a woman. Nor does what he said force us to deny Christ's mother: "Woman, what have you to do with me? My hour has not yet come" (John 2:4). Rather, it warns us to understand that according to his divinity he had no mother, for he was preparing to reveal the person of his majesty when he turned water into wine. But he was crucified according to his humanity, and that was the hour which had not yet come when he said, "What have you to do with me? My hour has not yet come"—that is, the hour in which I will acknowledge you. For then, as a man crucified, he recognized his mother and most humanely entrusted her to his beloved disciple. Nor should it trouble us that when his mother and brothers were announced to him, he answered, "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" and so on (Matthew 12:48). Rather, let it teach us that when parents hinder our ministry—the ministry by which we serve the word of God to our brothers and sisters—we ought not to acknowledge them. For if anyone thinks Christ had no mother on earth because he said, "Who is my mother?", then that person is forced to deny that the apostles had fathers on earth, since Christ commanded them, saying, "Do not call anyone father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven" (Matthew 23:9).

problems.source_quote: cuius maiestatis personam parabat ostendere aquam in uinum uertendo
problems.why: English reverses the relationship: Christ reveals his own majesty, not another's.
problems.fix: for he was preparing to reveal the person of his majesty when he turned water into wine

problems.quote: that is, the hour in which I will know you
problems.why: English 'I will know you' misses that Christ will acknowledge/recogize Mary as mother.
problems.fix: that is, the hour in which I will acknowledge you

problems.quote: Do not call anyone father to yourselves on earth
problems.source_quote: nolite nobis patrem dicere in terris
problems.why: 'nobis' = 'us', not 'yourselves'; Augustine quotes 'Do not call us father on earth'
problems.fix: Do not call us father on earth
problems.ruling: 'nobis' is dative/ablative plural 'us'; Augustine quotes Matt 23:9 with 'us' not 'yourselves'

problems.why: English adds 'as a human being' which is not in source; 'hominem' goes with 'crucifixus'.
problems.fix: then, crucified as a man, he recognized his mother
problems.ruling: 'cognouit hominem matrem' means 'recognized his human mother'; 'as a human being' wrongly attaches 'hominem' to manner, not to Mary.

problems.quote: Do not call us father on earth
problems.source_quote: nolite nobis patrem dicere in terris
problems.why: The Latin 'nobis' is dative 'to us,' but the command is 'Do not call [anyone] father to/for yourselves' (2nd person plural dative of advantage), not 'Do not call us father.' The English makes the apostles the fathers being denied.
problems.fix: Do not call anyone father on earth among yourselves

problems.quote: the apostle had fathers on earth
problems.source_quote: apostolus negare habuisse patres in terris
problems.why: The Latin 'patres' refers to spiritual fathers/ancestors (the apostles themselves as fathers in faith), not biological fathers; the argument is parallel to Christ's mother.
problems.fix: the apostle had spiritual fathers on earth

problems.quote: Do not call us father on earth
problems.source_quote: nolite nobis patrem dicere in terris
problems.why: 'nobis' here is dative of disadvantage ('call no one father on earth'), not 'call us father.' The English reverses the meaning.
problems.fix: Call no one father on earth
problems.ruling: 'nobis' is dative of disadvantage (for us/before us), meaning 'do not call anyone father for our benefit' or 'in relation to us'—the standard interpretation is 'call no one father,' not 'do not call us father.' The English reverses the meaning entirely.

problems.why: 'uirum gerendo' means 'bearing the role of husband/man,' not 'acting as a man' generally; context is Mary's husband Joseph through whom Christ was received.
problems.fix: by her husband's role, and being born of a woman
problems.ruling: 'uirum gerendo' refers to Joseph acting as husband; 'acting as a man' misleads readers about the incarnation context.
